---
<!-- question-1: body_md -->
Does every localization preserve the class of nilpotent groups?
<!-- end question-1 -->
<!-- question-2: body_md -->
For every localization $L$ and every finite $p$-group $G$,
is the map $G\to LG$ surjective?
<!-- end question-2 -->
<!-- theorem--1: body_md -->
For every odd prime $p$, there is a group $G$ of order $p^6$ and nilpotency class 3, with a local embedding $f \colon G \hookrightarrow H$ into an infinite non-nilpotent group. 
    Hence $L_f$ takes the nilpotent finite $p$-group $G$ to the infinite non-nilpotent group $H$.
<!-- end theorem--1 -->
<!-- question-3: body_md -->
Let $f\colon G \to H$ be a local homomorphism between finite groups. 
If $G$ is nilpotent, must $H$ be nilpotent?
<!-- end question-3 -->
<!-- question-4: body_md -->
If $G$ is a finite $2$-group, is it true that $LG$ is nilpotent for every localization $L$?
<!-- end question-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
For the group $G$ given by the presentation \eqref{eq:fin-rep} the following assertions hold:
    \begin{enumerate}\itemsep=0mm
        \item it is a finite group of order $p^6$;
        \item its derived subgroup $G'$ is cyclic of order $p^2$;
        \item its center is cyclic of order $p^2$;
        \item it is nilpotent of class 3.
    \end{enumerate}
    Furthermore, the centralizer $D := C(G') = \langle a, b^p \rangle$ has index $p$.
    This normal subgroup is the kernel of the map $\varepsilon: G \to \mathbb{Z}/p,\ a \mapsto 0, b \mapsto 1$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Only the last assertion remains.
    Clearly $a \in D$, while $b$ acts on $G'$ by multiplication by $1+p$ modulo $p^2$.
    Hence $a^ib^j \in D$ if and only if $p \mid j$, so $D = \langle a, b^p\rangle$ has index $p$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
This also works for $n = p^2$, since $p^2 \mid \binom{p^2}{2}$ and $p \mid \binom{p^2}{3}$:
    the map $x \mapsto x^{p^2}$ is an endomorphism of $G$ onto $Z(G)$.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
In $G$ the following equations hold:
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:3-5}
        (a^i b^j)^{p^3} = a^{p^2j}
    \end{equation}
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:3-6}
        (a^i b^{pk})^p = a^{pi} b^{p^2k}
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
The Frattini subgroup is $\Phi(G) = \langle a^p, b^p \rangle = \{ a^{pi} b^{pj}\}$, a group of order $p^4$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
For any finite $p$-group $X$ the Frattini subgroup is $\Phi(X) = X^p [X,X]$ (\cite[23.2, p. 105]{AschbacherFGT}).
    Equivalently, $N = \langle a^p, b^p\rangle$ is the kernel of $\pi \colon G \to \mathbb{F}_p^2,\ a^i b^j \mapsto (i \bmod p, j \bmod p)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:p-group-endomorphisms}
    For every endomorphism $\alpha : G \to G$ one of the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\alpha$ is an automorphism, $\xi \circ \alpha = \xi$ and $\alpha(q) = q^{(1+p)^d}$ for a unique $d \in \{ 0, 1, \ldots, p-1\}$;
        \item $\alpha(G') = 1$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Write $\alpha(a) = a^i b^j$ and $\alpha(b) = a^lb^m$.
    Since $\alpha(a)^{p^3} = 1$, \eqref{eq:3-5} gives $p \mid j$, say $j = pk$.
    Now $\alpha(a)^p = \alpha(q) \in G' = \langle q\rangle$, while $\alpha(a)^p = a^{pi}b^{p^2k}$ by \eqref{eq:3-6};
    by uniqueness of the normal form $p \mid k$, so $\alpha(a) = a^ic^s$ with $c = b^{p^2}$.

    Applying $\alpha$ to $a^{p^2} = b^{p^3}$ gives $a^{p^2i} = \alpha(a)^{p^2} = \alpha(b)^{p^3} = b^{p^3m} = a^{p^2m}$,
    so $i \equiv m \pmod p$.

    On the one hand, applying $\alpha$ to $[a,b] = a^p$ gives
    \begin{align}
        [a^i c^s, a^l b^m] &= [a^i, a^l b^m] = a^{-i} (a^l b^m)^{-1} a^i a^l b^m \notag\\
        &= a^{-i} b^{-m} a^i b^m = a^{i((1+p)^m - 1)}.
    \end{align}
    On the other hand,
    \begin{align}\label{eq:a-cubed}
        \alpha(a)^p = a^{pi}c^{ps} = a^{pi + p^2s}
    \end{align}
    Hence,
    \begin{align}\label{eq:second-congruence}
    i((1+p)^m-1) \equiv pi + p^2s \pmod {p^3}.
    \end{align}
    Dividing by $p$ and reducing modulo $p$, using $\frac{(1+p)^m-1}{p} \equiv m \pmod p$, we get $i(m-1) \equiv 0 \pmod p$.
    As $m \equiv i \pmod p$, this gives $i(i-1) \equiv 0 \pmod p$, so $i \equiv 0$ or $i \equiv 1 \pmod p$.

    \noindent \textit{Case $i \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$}.
    Then $m \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
    Consider the induced map $\bar{\alpha} : \mathbb{F}_p^2 \to \mathbb{F}_p^2$:
    \begin{align*}
        \alpha(a) = a^i c^s & \mapsto (i, 0) = i \bar{a};\\
        \alpha(b) = a^l b^m & \mapsto l \bar{a} + m\bar{b}.
    \end{align*}
    Writing the matrix of $\bar{\alpha}$ in the basis $\bar{a}, \bar{b}$, we get
    \[ M = \begin{pmatrix}
        i & l \\
        0 & m \\
    \end{pmatrix} \quad \det M = im. \]
    We have $i \equiv m \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$,
    so $\det M \ne 0$ and $\bar\alpha$ is bijective, i.e. $\alpha(G)\Phi(G) = G$.
    Since the elements of $\Phi(G)$ are non-generators, $\alpha(G) = G$, and $\alpha$ is bijective because $G$ is finite.
    By \eqref{eq:a-cubed}, $\alpha(q) = q^{i+ps}$ with $i + ps \equiv 1 \pmod p$;
    modulo $p^2$ the elements congruent to $1$ modulo $p$ are exactly the powers $(1+p)^d$, $0 \le d < p$, since $(1+p)^d \equiv 1+pd \pmod{p^2}$.
    Thus $\alpha(q) = q^{(1+p)^d}$ for a unique $d \in \{ 0, 1, \ldots, p-1 \}$.

    Finally, for all $u, v \in \mathbb{Z}$
    \begin{align*}
        \xi(\alpha(a^v b^u)) &= \alpha(a^v b^u)^{p^3} = (\alpha(a)^v \alpha(b)^u)^{p^3} \\
        &= (a^{v i} c^{v s} (a^l b^m)^u)^{p^3} = (b^{p^3})^{mu} = a^{p^2u m}.
    \end{align*}
    Using that $m \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, we have $p^2m u \equiv p^2u \pmod{p^3}$.
    Hence $\xi\circ\alpha = \xi$.

    \noindent \textit{Case $i \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$}.
    Then $m \equiv 0 \pmod p$, so $(1+p)^m \equiv 1 \pmod{p^2}$.
    Together with $p \mid i$, we get from the congruence \eqref{eq:second-congruence} that $pi + p^2s \equiv 0 \pmod{p^3}$.
    Thus $\alpha(q) = a^{pi + p^2s} = 1$, and $\alpha$ kills $G'$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{remark:xi-notation}
    Since $\xi(g) = a^{p^2\varepsilon(g)}$, the identity $\xi\circ\alpha = \xi$ gives
    $\varepsilon\circ\alpha = \varepsilon$ for every automorphism $\alpha$ of $G$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:simple-monster}
    There is a graded set $\mathcal{R}\subseteq N$ with normal closure $R \subseteq F$ such that the groups $T = F/R$ and $S = N/R$ satisfy
    \begin{enumerate}\itemsep=0mm
        \item $\langle F \mid \mathcal{R} \rangle$ is graded diagrammatically aspherical;
        \item $S$ is an infinite simple torsion-free group with every proper subgroup cyclic;
        \item the conjugation action of $T$ on $S$ identifies $\operatorname{Aut}(S) = T$ and conjugation by $t$ is regular (in particular, $\operatorname{Out}(S) = C_p$);
        \item every finite subgroup of $T$ is conjugate into $\langle t \rangle$.
    \end{enumerate}
    Moreover, there are integers $n \ge 1$ and $h \ge 2$ such that $\mathcal{R}$ contains words $r_5, r_6, r_7 \in \langle x, y\rangle$ with $\exp_y(r_k) = h - 2$ and
     \begin{align}
        \exp_x(r_k) = hn + k(h-1) + 15(h-1)(h-2) 
    \end{align}
    for $k = 5, 6, 7$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
We apply Obraztsov's theorems with $G_1 = \langle x\rangle$, $G_2 = \langle y\rangle$, $G_3 = H = C_p = \langle t\rangle$, $m = \infty$, $g_1, g_2$ trivial and $g_3$ the identity. 
Since $p$ is odd, all three factors have no involutions. 
Then $G(1) = F$, the images of the $g_i$ generate $H$, and $N_1 = \langle x\rangle$, $N_2 = \langle y\rangle$ are non-trivial. 
Theorems A, B and D give a presentation $T := \langle G(1) \mid \mathcal{R}\rangle$ and a normal subgroup $S := L$ of $T$, infinite and simple, with $T/S \cong C_p$.

Let $\tau\colon F \to T$ and $\kappa\colon T \to T/S$ be the natural projections, so that $R = \ker\tau$ is the normal closure of $\mathcal{R}$, and let $\rho = \kappa\circ\tau\colon F \to T/S \cong C_p$.
By Theorem A(1), $x$ and $y$ map into $S$, so their normal closure $N$ lies in $\ker\rho$;
both have index $p$, as $\pi$ and $\rho$ are onto, so $N = \ker\rho$ and in particular $\mathcal{R} \subseteq N$. 
Moreover, $\tau^{-1}(S) = \ker\rho = N$ and $\tau$ is onto, so $S = \tau(N) = N/R$.

It remains to prove items (2)--(4) and the final assertion. 
Since all $G_i$ are cyclic, Theorem D shows that every proper subgroup of $S$ is cyclic. 
For torsion-freeness, let $X \in S$ be non-trivial. 
If $X$ is conjugate into $\langle x\rangle$ or $\langle y\rangle$, it has infinite order; 
it is not conjugate into $\langle t\rangle$, as its image in $T/S$ would be non-trivial. 
Otherwise, since $C_p$ has no elements of even order, Theorem A(2) shows that $X$ has infinite order.

Item (3) is Theorem A(3), and regularity follows from Theorem B. 
For item (4), let $A \subseteq T$ be finite. 
Since $S$ is torsion-free, $A \cap S = 1$, so $A$ embeds into $T/S \cong C_p$; 
hence $A = \langle u\rangle$ is cyclic. 
By Lemma~\ref{lemma:conjugate-into}, $u$ is conjugate to an element of $\langle x\rangle$, $\langle y\rangle$ or $\langle t\rangle$, and only the last is possible, since $\langle x\rangle$ and $\langle y\rangle$ are torsion-free. 
So $A$ is conjugate into $\langle t\rangle$.

The words $r_k$ are relators of the second type \cite[(2.2), p.~277]{Obraztsov}:
\[r_k = c^{-1}A^n c A^{n+k} c A^{n + 30 + k} \ldots c A^{n + 30(h-2) + k}\]
for suitable elements $a, c$, where $A = a(aca^{-1}c^{-1})^{\ell} = a[a^{-1},c^{-1}]^{\ell}$ with $\ell \geq 1$ is a period (Obraztsov writes commutators as $uvu^{-1}v^{-1}$, so this is his $a[a,c]^{\ell}$);
that one may take this word to be a period is \cite[p.~277]{Obraztsov}, which refers to \cite[Lemma~3.1]{Obraztsov1994}.
We can take $a = x$ and $c = y$. 
For this we well-order $I_1$ so that $\langle x\rangle$ precedes $\langle y\rangle$, and choose the ordering of $\Omega$ so that $x$ is its least element; 
then $x$ is the minimal element of $F(\{A\})$, as required before \cite[(2.2)]{Obraztsov}.
We also take $h = \delta^{-1} \ge 2$ and $n = [n_0/(h+1)]$, with $\delta$, $n_0$ as in \cite[\S2, p.~276]{Obraztsov}. 
Then $\exp_x(A) = 1$ and $\exp_y(A) = 0$, so $\exp_y(r_k) = h - 2$ and 
\[ \exp_x(r_k) = n + \sum_{j = 0}^{h-2}{(n + 30j + k)} = hn + k(h-1) + 15(h-1)(h-2). \]
These relators exist for $5 \le k \le 15$; in particular $r_5, r_6, r_7$ are available.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{remark:endomorphism-dichotomy}
    As for any simple group, every endomorphism $f\colon S \to S$ is either trivial or injective. 
    If $f$ is injective, then $f(S) \cong S$ is not cyclic, so $f(S)$ is not a proper subgroup and $f$ is an automorphism. 
    Hence every endomorphism of $S$ is either trivial or an automorphism.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
A central extension of a group $Y$ is a surjective homomorphism $X \twoheadrightarrow Y$ with its kernel contained in the center.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
A group $X$ is called \emph{perfect} if it is equal to its own commutator subgroup: $X = [X, X]$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma:uniqueness-map}
    Let $\pi: Y \to X$ be a central extension and $Z$ be a perfect group.
    If two homomorphisms $f_1, f_2 : Z \to Y$ are such that $\pi \circ f_1 = \pi \circ f_2$, then $f_1 = f_2$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Put $d(a) = f_1(a)^{-1} f_2(a)$. 
    By assumption $\pi \circ d = 1$, so the image of $d$ lies in the kernel of $\pi$ and is thus central.
    Hence $d$ is a homomorphism: $d(ab) = f_1(b)^{-1} d(a) f_2(b) = d(a) d(b)$ since $d(a)$ is central. 
    Since its image is abelian, $d$ factors through the abelianization of $Z$, which is trivial because $Z$ is perfect. Hence $d$ is trivial and $f_1 = f_2$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma:modified-relator-count}
    Choose a relator $r_0 \in \mathcal{R}$ that is not a proper power in $F$. 
    There is a homomorphism 
    \[\lambda: R/[R,R] \to \mathbb{Z}[C_p]\] satisfying
    \begin{enumerate}\itemsep=0mm
        \item $\lambda(r^f) = \lambda(r) t^{\pi(f)}$ for any $ r\in R, f\in F$;
        \item $\lambda(r_0) = 1$ and $\lambda(r) = 0$ for any $r\in \mathcal{R}$ not conjugate to $r_0^{\pm 1}$.
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Lemma~\ref{lemma:counting-relators} assumes that no relator is conjugate to another relator or to its inverse. 
    We may assume this for Obraztsov's presentation: within one rank we discard duplicates, and across ranks it cannot happen, by asphericity. 
    The lemma gives $\lambda_{r_0}\colon R/[R,R] \to \mathbb{Z}[T]$, and we compose it with the map $\mathbb{Z}[T] \to \mathbb{Z}[C_p]$ induced by $T \to C_p$, which exists because $R \subseteq N = \ker\pi$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:K-perfect-extension}
    The group $K$ is a perfect central extension of $S$. 
    Moreover, $Z(K) = \langle z \rangle \cong C_{p^2}$ and coincides with the set of torsion elements of $K$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $A := R / \ker \chi$.
    First note that $\chi$ is onto, so by the first isomorphism theorem $A \cong C_{p^2}$.
    For $n \in N$ and $r \in R$ we have $\chi(r^n) = \chi(r)$, since $N = \ker\pi$; 
    hence $[R,N] \subseteq \ker\chi$.
    Therefore, $A$ is central in $K$ and is generated by $z$ since $\chi(w) = 1$.

    By the third isomorphism theorem, $K/A \cong N/R \cong S$, which has trivial center, so $Z(K) = A$.
    In particular, $K$ is a central extension of $S$ as there is the short exact sequence 
    \[ 1 \to Z(K) \cong C_{p^2} \to K \to S \to 1. \]
    Since $w \in [N,N]$, we have $z \in [K,K]$, so $Z(K) \subseteq [K,K]$; as $K/Z(K) \cong S$ is perfect, so is $K$.
    
    For the last claim, suppose $k \in K$ has finite order. 
    Its image in $S$ has finite order, hence is trivial because $S$ is torsion-free (Proposition~\ref{prop:simple-monster}(2)); so $k \in Z(K)$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{remark:action-on-z}
    We have $K_1 = K \rtimes \langle t\rangle$, since $K$ is normal of index $p$ and $t \notin K$ has order $p$. 
    Moreover, $z^t = z^{1+p}$: since $w^t \in R$, $\chi(w^t) = (1+p)^{\pi(t)}\chi(w) = 1+p$ and $\chi$ induces $Z(K) \cong \mathbb{Z} / p^2$. 
    In other words, $t$ acts on $Z(K)$ as multiplication by $1+p$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:k-endomorphisms}
    Every automorphism of $K$ is conjugation by an element of $K_1$, that is, of the form $\beta^e\circ c_k$ with $e \in \{0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$ and $k \in K$. 
    Every non-trivial endomorphism of $K$ is an automorphism.
    
    Moreover, if $\beta(k) k^{-1} \in Z(K)$, then $k \in Z(K)$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $\psi \in \operatorname{Aut}(K)$.
    It has to preserve the center $Z(K)$, so it induces an automorphism $\psi'$ of $S$.
    By Proposition~\ref{prop:simple-monster}(3), $\psi'$ is conjugation by some $\tau \in T$.
    Since $\ker\chi \subseteq R$, the projection $\sigma_1\colon K_1 \to T$ is onto; let $\tau_1$ be a preimage of $\tau$.
    The projection $\sigma_1$ restricts to $\sigma$, so  
    \[ \sigma \circ c_{\tau_1} = \sigma \circ \psi.\]
    Then Lemma~\ref{lemma:uniqueness-map} says $\psi = c_{\tau_1}$.

    Now suppose $\psi$ is a non-trivial endomorphism.
    By Proposition~\ref{prop:K-perfect-extension}, $Z(K)$ is the set of elements of finite order,
    so $\psi$ maps $Z(K)$ to itself.
    Hence, $\psi$ induces an endomorphism $\psi'$ of $S$.
    By Remark~\ref{remark:endomorphism-dichotomy} there are two possibilities: $\psi'$ is an automorphism or $\psi'$ is trivial. 
    If it is trivial, then $\psi(K) \subseteq Z(K)$ is abelian and $\psi$ kills $K = [K, K]$, in other words, $\psi$ is trivial.
    If $\psi'$ is an automorphism, the argument above shows that $\psi$ is conjugation by an element of $K_1$.

    For the last claim, the assumption says the image of $k$ in $S$ is fixed by conjugation by $t$, so the image must be trivial by Proposition~\ref{prop:simple-monster}(3).
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma:comm-is-perfect}
    We have $K = [H,H]$.
    In particular, $H$ is not solvable, and hence not nilpotent.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The subgroup $K$ is the kernel of the surjection $p_1\colon H_1 \to G$, $gk \mapsto g$, which sends $qz^{-1}$ to $q$; 
    so $p_1(K\Delta) = \langle q\rangle$ and
    \[ H / K \cong (H_1 / \Delta) / (K\Delta / \Delta) \cong H_1 / K\Delta \cong G / (p_1(K\Delta)) = G / \langle q \rangle = G / G'.\] 
    Hence $[H,H] \subseteq K$, and conversely $K = [K,K] \subseteq [H,H]$ because $K$ is perfect.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma:conjugate-into-g}
    Every finite subgroup of $H$ lies in a conjugate of $G$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Consider the map $\rho_1 : H_1 \to T$ given by $\rho_1(gk) = t^{\varepsilon(g)} \sigma(k)$. 
    It is a homomorphism: 
    \begin{align*}
    \rho_1(g_1 k_1 g_2 k_2) = \rho_1(g_1g_2 \beta^{\varepsilon(g_2)}(k_1) k_2) = t^{\varepsilon(g_1g_2)} \sigma(\beta^{\varepsilon(g_2)}(k_1) k_2) = \\
    = t^{\varepsilon(g_1)} t^{\varepsilon(g_2)} t^{-\varepsilon(g_2)} \sigma(k_1) t^{\varepsilon(g_2)} \sigma(k_2) 
    = \rho_1(g_1 k_1) \rho_1(g_2 k_2).  
    \end{align*}
    (We used that $K_1 \to T$ restricts to $\sigma$ and fixes $t$.) 
    Since $\varepsilon(q) = 0$ and $\sigma(z) = 1$, $\rho_1(qz^{-1}) = 1$, 
    so $\rho_1$ factors through $\rho\colon H \to T$. 
    It is surjective, since $\rho(b) = t$, $\rho(K) = S$ and $T = S\langle t\rangle$.
    
    Observe that $\rho^{-1}(\langle t \rangle) = G$.
    Indeed, if $\rho(gk) \in \langle t\rangle$ then $\sigma(k) = 1$ using that $S \cap \langle t \rangle = 1$.
    Thus $k\in Z(K) = \langle z \rangle$ and $z = q \in G$ in $H$, so $gk \in G$.

    Now suppose $A \subseteq H$ is finite. 
    Then $B := \rho(A)$ is a finite subgroup of $T$ and by Proposition~\ref{prop:simple-monster}(4)  it is conjugate into $\langle t \rangle$ by some $u \in T$, in other words $B^u \subseteq \langle t \rangle$.
    Choose $h\in H$ with $\rho(h) = u$.
    Then $A^h \subseteq (\rho^{-1}B)^h = \rho^{-1}(B^u) \subseteq \rho^{-1}\langle t \rangle \subseteq G$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
Every homomorphism $G \to H$ extends to exactly one endomorphism of $H$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Suppose $\alpha: G \to H$ is a homomorphism.
    Its image is finite, so by Lemma~\ref{lemma:conjugate-into-g} it lies in $uGu^{-1}$ for some $u \in H$; replacing $\alpha$ by $c_u\circ\alpha$, we may assume $\alpha(G) \subseteq G$.
    
    \emph{Existence}.     
    By Proposition~\ref{prop:p-group-endomorphisms}, $\alpha$ either kills $G'$ or is an automorphism.
    If $\alpha$ is an automorphism, then $\varepsilon \circ \alpha = \varepsilon$ and $\alpha(q) = q^{(1+p)^d}$ for some $d$. 
    Put 
    \[ \theta_\alpha : H_1 \to H_1\quad \theta_\alpha(gk) = \alpha(g) \cdot \beta^d(k). \] 
    It is a homomorphism: on one side
    \begin{align*}
        \theta_\alpha(g_1 k_1 g_2 k_2) = \theta_\alpha(g_1 g_2 \beta^{\varepsilon(g_2)}(k_1) k_2) = \alpha(g_1 g_2) \beta^{d+ \varepsilon(g_2)}(k_1) \beta^{d}(k_2);
    \end{align*}
    and on the other 
    \begin{align*}
        \theta_\alpha(g_1 k_1) \theta_\alpha(g_2 k_2) = 
        \alpha(g_1) \beta^d(k_1) \alpha(g_2) \beta^d(k_2) = \\ 
        = \alpha(g_1) \alpha(g_2) \beta^{\varepsilon(\alpha(g_2))}(\beta^d(k_1)) \beta^d(k_2)
    \end{align*}
    Using that $\varepsilon \circ \alpha = \varepsilon$, we see the two expressions coincide.
    It is bijective: the inverse homomorphism is built in the same way from $\alpha^{-1}$.
    
    By Remark~\ref{remark:action-on-z},
    \[ \theta_\alpha(qz^{-1}) = \alpha(q)\beta^d(z)^{-1} = q^{(1+p)^d} z^{-(1+p)^d} = (qz^{-1})^{(1+p)^d}, \]
    so $\theta_\alpha$ maps $\Delta$ onto itself ($(1+p)^d$ is a unit modulo $p^2$) and induces an automorphism of $H$, which extends $\alpha$ because $\theta_\alpha(g) = \alpha(g)$ for $g \in G$. 
    If $\alpha$ kills $G'$, it factors as $G \to G/G' \to G$, and the composite $H \to H/K \cong G/G' \to G$ extends $\alpha$, since $g \mapsto gG' \mapsto \alpha(g)$.
    
    \emph{Uniqueness}. 
    Let $\theta$ be an endomorphism extending $\alpha$.
    Since $K = [H, H]$, $\theta(K) = \theta([H,H]) \subseteq [H,H] = K$, and $\theta|_K$ is either trivial or an automorphism by Proposition~\ref{prop:k-endomorphisms}.

    If $\alpha$ kills $G'$, then $\theta(z) = \theta(q) = \alpha(q) = 1$, so $\theta|_K$ is not injective and has to be trivial. 
    So $\theta$ is determined by its values on $G$ and $K$, which generate $H$.

    Suppose $\alpha$ is an automorphism. 
    By replacing $\theta$ by $\theta \circ \theta_\alpha^{-1}$, we may assume $\theta$ fixes $G$ pointwise. 
    Then $\theta(z) = \theta(q) = q = z$, so $\theta|_K$ is non-trivial, hence bijective. 
    Write $\theta|_K = \beta^e \circ c_k$ with $k\in K$ and $e \in \{ 0,1,\ldots,p-1\}$. 

    First, observe that the condition $z = \theta(z) = \beta^e(c_k(z)) = \beta^e(z) = z^{(1+p)^e}$ forces $e = 0$, since $1+p$ has order $p$ modulo $p^2$, so $\theta|_K = c_k$. 
    Second, since $\theta$ fixes $b$, $\theta|_K$ commutes with $\beta$:
    $\theta|_K(\beta(m)) = \theta|_K(m^b) = \theta|_K(m)^{\theta(b)} = \theta|_K(m)^b$.
    Thus $c_k\circ\beta = \beta\circ c_k = c_{\beta(k)}\circ\beta$, and since $\beta$ is surjective, $c_k = c_{\beta(k)}$, i.e. $\beta(k)k^{-1} \in Z(K)$. 
    By Proposition~\ref{prop:k-endomorphisms}, $k \in Z(K)$, so $\theta|_K = \operatorname{id}$.
    Since $\theta$ is the identity on $K$ and on $G$, $\theta$ has to be the identity.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
For every odd prime $p$, there are a group $G$ of order $p^6$ and class 3, a countably infinite non-nilpotent group $H$ and a local embedding $f\colon G \to H$. 
    In particular, $L_fG \cong H$, so the localization $L_f$ does not preserve nilpotency.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
A cell decomposition $\Delta$ of an oriented surface $X$ is called a \emph{map} on $X$.
The orientation on $X$ defines an orientation of $\Delta$: we consider edges of $\Delta$ to be oriented; thus, with every edge $e$ of $\Delta$ there is the associated edge $e^{-1}$ with the opposite orientation. 

If $X$ is a disc (a sphere), $\Delta$ is called \emph{circular} (\emph{spherical}).
The boundary of a circular $\Delta$ is always traversed clockwise.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
If a component of the boundary consists of edges $e_1\ldots e_n$ listed in accordance with the orientation, then the path $e_1\ldots e_n$ is a loop and it is called the \emph{contour} of $\Delta$.
Similarly, we define the contour of any cell $\Pi$, denoted $\partial \Pi$.
We consider contours up to a cyclic shift. 
A circular $\Delta$ has a single contour.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
A map $\Delta$ equipped with an assignment $e \mapsto \phi(e) \in \mathcal{A}^{1}$ is called a \emph{diagram over} $\mathcal{A}$ if $\phi(e^{-1}) = \phi(e)^{-1}$ for any edge $e$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
Consider a path $p = e_1 \ldots e_n$ in a diagram $\Delta$ over $\mathcal{A}$. 
Define its \emph{label} as $\phi(p) := \phi(e_1) \ldots \phi(e_n)$. 
If $n = 0$, by convention $\phi(p) = 1$.  
The label of a contour of a cell or a diagram is defined up to cyclic shift, in other words, it is a cyclic word. 
Two words are \emph{visually equal}, written $\equiv$, if they coincide letter by letter.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
A cell of a diagram $\Delta$ is called an $\mathcal{R}$-cell if the label $\phi(p)$ of its contour is visually equal (up to cyclic conjugacy) to some word $R \in \mathcal{R}$ or $R^{-1}$, or to some word obtained from $R, R^{-1}$ by insertions of the symbol 1.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- definition-8: body_md -->
\label{def:0-cells}
    A cell $\Pi$ is called a 0-cell if either the label of its contour $e_1\ldots e_n$ is visually equal to $\phi(e_1) \ldots \phi(e_n)$ with $\phi(e_i) \equiv 1$, or, for some $i \neq j$, $\phi(e_i) \equiv a, \phi(e_j) \equiv a^{-1}, \phi(e_k) \equiv 1$ for any $k \neq i, j$. 
    Such a label is $1$ in the free group.
    Edges labelled 1 are called \emph{0-edges}; the others are called \emph{$\mathcal{A}$-edges}.
<!-- end definition-8 -->
<!-- definition-9: body_md -->
A diagram on a surface $X$ over a presentation \eqref{eq:rep} is any diagram over the alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ whose cells are $\mathcal{R}$-cells or 0-cells.
<!-- end definition-9 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
Let $W$ be an arbitrary non-empty word in the alphabet $\mathcal{A}^1$.
    Then $W = 1$ in the group $G$ with presentation \eqref{eq:rep} if and only if there exists a circular diagram over \eqref{eq:rep} whose contour label is visually equal to $W$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- definition-10: body_md -->
Let $\mathcal{R}$ be a set of words in a group alphabet $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{A}^{-1}$ and suppose it is decomposed into subsets $\mathcal{R} = \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} \mathcal{R}_i$ in such a way that a word in $\mathcal{R}_i$ cannot coincide with a cyclic conjugate of a word in $\mathcal{R}_j$ or its inverse if $i \neq j$.
    Then the presentation $\langle \mathcal{A} \mid \mathcal{R} = \bigcup \mathcal{R}_i \rangle$ is called a \emph{graded} presentation, the members of $\mathcal{R}_i$ are called \emph{relators of rank} $i$.
<!-- end definition-10 -->
<!-- definition-11: body_md -->
If two words $X$ and $Y$ are equal in the group 
    \[ G(i) = \left\langle \mathcal{A} \mid R = 1, R \in \bigcup_{j = 1}^{i} \mathcal{R}_j \right\rangle, \]
    then we say $X$ and $Y$ are equal in rank $i$ and write $X \overset{i}{=} Y$.
<!-- end definition-11 -->
<!-- definition-12: body_md -->
A map $\Delta$ is \emph{graded} if it is equipped with an assignment of rank to each of its cells. 
    The rank of a cell $\Pi$ is denoted $r(\Pi)$. 

    A diagram is graded if its underlying map is graded. 
    There is a natural grading for a diagram over a graded presentation:
    an $\mathcal{R}$-cell whose contour label is obtained from a relator $R \in \mathcal{R}_i$ as in the definition of an $\mathcal{R}$-cell gets rank $r(\Pi) = i$, which is well defined by the definition of a graded presentation, and 0-cells get rank $0$.
<!-- end definition-12 -->
<!-- definition-13: body_md -->
For $j \geq 1$ a pair of cells $\Pi_1, \Pi_2$ of rank $j$ is said to be cancellable in a diagram $\Delta$, or a \emph{$j$-pair}, if there is a 0-refinement $\Delta'$ containing copies $\Pi_1', \Pi_2'$ of $\Pi_1, \Pi_2$ and 
    a path $t$ without self-intersections joining a vertex $O_1$ of $\Pi_1'$ to a vertex $O_2$ of $\Pi_2'$ such that $\phi(t) \overset{j-1}{=} 1$ and $\phi(p_1) = \phi(p_2)^{-1}$ in $F$, where $p_1$ and $p_2$ are the contours of $\Pi_1'$ and $\Pi_2'$ starting at $O_1$ and $O_2$ (both traversed clockwise).
<!-- end definition-13 -->
<!-- definition-14: body_md -->
A graded diagram is said to be reduced if it does not contain a $j$-pair for any $j \geq 1$.
<!-- end definition-14 -->
<!-- definition-15: body_md -->
The \emph{rank} of a diagram is the largest rank of its cells.
    Its \emph{type} $\tau = (\tau_1, \tau_2, \ldots )$ is a sequence where $\tau_i$ is the number of cells of rank $i$ in the diagram.
<!-- end definition-15 -->
<!-- definition-16: body_md -->
A graded presentation of $G$ is called \emph{diagrammatically aspherical} or simply \emph{aspherical} if every graded spherical diagram over it is either non-reduced or consists entirely of 0-cells.
<!-- end definition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma:counting-relators}
  Let $G = \langle F \mid \mathcal{R} \rangle$ be a graded aspherical presentation over a free product $F$ of groups without involutions, with kernel $N$, satisfying the conventions above.
  Regard the relation module $N_{\mathrm{ab}} = N/[N,N]$ as a right $\mathbb{Z}G$-module via $(u[N,N])\cdot\bar f = u^f[N,N]$.
  Let $R_0 \in \mathcal{R}$ be a relator that is not a proper power in $F$.
  Then $R_0[N,N]$ generates a free $\mathbb{Z}G$-submodule of rank one of $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$, and this submodule is a direct summand of $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$.
  More precisely, there is a unique homomorphism $\lambda : N \to \mathbb{Z}G$ such that
  \begin{enumerate}\itemsep=0mm
    \item $\lambda(u^f) = \lambda(u)\,\bar f$ for all $u \in N$, $f \in F$;
    \item $\lambda(R_0) = 1$;
    \item $\lambda(r) = 0$ for every $r \in \mathcal{R} \setminus \{R_0\}$;
  \end{enumerate}
  it induces a $\mathbb{Z}G$-linear map $\bar\lambda\colon N_{\mathrm{ab}} \to \mathbb{Z}G$ which splits $x \mapsto R_0[N,N]\cdot x$.
  In particular, if no relator in $\mathcal{R}$ is a proper power in $F$, then $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$ is a free $\mathbb{Z}G$-module with basis $\{R[N,N] : R \in \mathcal{R}\}$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We follow the counting argument of \cite[Lemma~32.2]{Olshanskii}, but assign each cell its position in $G$ instead of grouping cells into equivalence classes.

  \emph{Vertex labels.}
  In a disc or spherical diagram with a fixed base vertex, label each vertex $v$ by $b(v) = \overline{\phi(g)} \in G$, where $g$ is any path from the base to $v$.
  This does not depend on $g$: the label of a closed path is trivial in $G$, because every cell label is.

  \emph{Weights.}
  A cell gets weight $0$ unless its contour label $W$, read from some vertex $v$, satisfies $W = c R_0^{\varepsilon} c^{-1}$ in $F$ with $\varepsilon = \pm 1$.
  In that case its weight is
  \[ \omega = \varepsilon\, \bar c^{-1}\, b(v)^{-1} \in \mathbb{Z}G . \]
  The sign is unique, because $R_0$ is not conjugate to $R_0^{-1}$ in $F$.
  Indeed, suppose $g^{-1}R_0g = R_0^{-1}$ for some $g \in F$; then $g^2$ centralizes $R_0$.
  The centralizer of $R_0$ is $\langle R_0 \rangle$ \cite[Theorem~33.4]{Olshanskii}, since $R_0$ has infinite order, is not conjugate into a factor and is not a proper power.
  Hence $g^2 = R_0^k$ for some $k$, and conjugating by $g$ gives $R_0^k = g^{-1}g^2g = (g^{-1}R_0g)^k = R_0^{-k}$.
  Since $R_0$ has infinite order, $k = 0$, so $g^2 = 1$.
  Then $g = 1$, because $F$ has no involutions (every element of finite order in $F$ is conjugate into a factor), and $R_0 = R_0^{-1}$, which is impossible.

  The weight does not depend on the choices.
  Another conjugator differs from $c$ by an element of $C_F(R_0) = \langle R_0 \rangle \subseteq N$, so $\bar c$ is unchanged.
  Moving the starting vertex along a boundary segment $s$ replaces $c$ by $s^{-1}c$ and $b(v)$ by $b(v)\bar s$, so $\omega$ is unchanged.
  $0$-refinements do not change any weight.


  \emph{Collars.} If two words $W_1, W_2$ are equal in $F$, the van Kampen Lemma for the presentation of $F$ without relators gives a disc of 0-cells with contour label $W_1\,1\,W_2^{-1}\,1$. Identifying its two edges labelled $1$, as in the proof of \cite[Lemma~11.2]{Olshanskii}, gives an annulus of 0-cells, a \emph{collar}: its outer contour has label $W_1$, its inner boundary read clockwise has label $W_2$, and a 0-edge joins their starting vertices. Unlike a 0-refinement, attaching a collar changes the contour label, but only to a word equal in $F$. It adds only cells of weight $0$, and if the base vertex is joined to the new one by 0-edges, it changes no vertex label.

  \emph{Spherical diagrams have total weight $0$.}
  We argue by induction on the type of the diagram, as in \cite[\S 13.2]{Olshanskii}.
  If there are no cells of positive rank, the total weight is $0$.
  Otherwise asphericity provides a $j$-pair.
  Its connecting path is trivial in rank $j-1$, hence in $G$, so the starting vertices of the two cells have the same label.
  Read from $O_1$ and $O_2$, their contour labels are mutually inverse in $F$, so if one is $cR_0^{\varepsilon}c^{-1}$ the other is $cR_0^{-\varepsilon}c^{-1}$, and their weights are opposite (or both $0$).
  
  Choose the base vertex outside the part of the diagram that is changed. After attaching collars, we may assume that the two based contour labels are visually $P$ and $P^{-1}$. Cancelling the pair replaces a disc with contour label $P\,U\,P^{-1}U^{-1}$, where $U = \phi(t) \overset{j-1}{=} 1$, by a disc of rank $<j$. The removed pair has total weight $0$.  
  Take for the new disc two mirror copies of a rank-$(j-1)$ diagram for $U = 1$, joined by a strip labelled $P$ \cite[Fig.~87]{Olshanskii}.
  Since $\overline{P} = 1$, corresponding cells of the two copies have the same vertex labels and opposite orientations, so their weights cancel.
  The total weight is therefore unchanged, while the type decreases.

  \emph{Definition of $\lambda$.}
  For $u \in N$, let $\lambda(u)$ be the total weight of a disc diagram whose contour label represents $u$ (based at the start of the contour).
  Given two such discs, attach a collar to one of them so that the two contour labels become visually equal with the same starting vertex; gluing them along the contour gives a sphere of total weight $\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 0$, so $\lambda$ is well defined.
  Placing two discs side by side shows $\lambda(u_1u_2) = \lambda(u_1) + \lambda(u_2)$, since $\bar u_1 = 1$.
  A whisker labelled $f^{-1}$ turns a disc for $u$ into a disc for $u^f$ and left-multiplies every vertex label by $\bar f^{-1}$; this gives (1).
  One-cell diagrams give (2) and (3); for (3), recall that no relator other than $R_0$ is conjugate to $R_0^{\pm1}$.
  Uniqueness holds because $N$ is generated by the conjugates of relators.

  \emph{The relation module.}
  Since the additive group of $\mathbb{Z}G$ is abelian, $\lambda$ vanishes on $[N,N]$, and by (1) the induced map $\bar\lambda\colon N_{\mathrm{ab}} \to \mathbb{Z}G$ is $\mathbb{Z}G$-linear.
  By (2), $\bar\lambda(R_0[N,N]\cdot x) = \bar\lambda(R_0[N,N])\,x = x$ for all $x \in \mathbb{Z}G$.
  Hence $x \mapsto R_0[N,N]\cdot x$ is injective, and its image is a free direct summand of rank one, with complement $\ker\bar\lambda$.
  For the last assertion, the elements $R[N,N]$, $R \in \mathcal{R}$, generate $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$, again because $N$ is generated by the conjugates of relators.
  If $\sum_{R} R[N,N]\cdot x_R = 0$, then applying $\bar\lambda$ for the relator $R_0$ and using (2) and (3) gives $x_{R_0} = 0$; this holds for every $R_0 \in \mathcal{R}$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
For graded aspherical presentations over a free group, the last assertion of Lemma~\ref{lemma:counting-relators} is \cite[Corollary~32.1]{Olshanskii}; see also \cite[Theorem~5 and Corollary~3]{AshmanovOlshanskii}.
  Lemma~\ref{lemma:counting-relators} is its analogue over free products, with the hypothesis imposed only on the relator $R_0$; this is all that Section~\ref{section:the-central-extension} needs.
  When no relator is a proper power, the statement that every spherical diagram has total weight $0$ for every choice of $R_0$ is the identity property of \cite[Definition~3.1]{Hitchman} for the pair formed by presentation complexes of $G$ and of $F$, and the freeness of $N_{\mathrm{ab}}$ then also follows from \cite[Proposition~3.4]{Hitchman}.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- definition-17: body_md -->
The \emph{free amalgam} of a family of groups $\{ X_i \}_{i\in I}$ is the (set) union $\bigcup X_i$.
    We take this union to be ``disjoint'' in the sense that $X_i \cap X_j = \{ 1 \}$ whenever $i \neq j$.
    We will call a map out of an amalgam into a group an \emph{embedding} if it is injective and a homomorphism restricted to each $X_i$.
<!-- end definition-17 -->
<!-- obra-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:A}
    Let $m$ be a sufficiently large odd number or $m = \infty$, and let $g_i\colon G_i \to H$ be homomorphisms with kernels $N_i$ whose images generate $H$. 
    Suppose that the set $I_1$ of indices $j$ with $N_j \ne 1$ has more than one element, let $\Omega^1_1$ be the free amalgam of $\{N_j\}_{j\in I_1}$, 
    and let $f\colon 2^\Omega \setminus \{\emptyset\} \to 2^\Omega$ be a generating map such that $f(C) \cap \Omega_1 \neq \emptyset$ whenever $C$ is not contained in a single factor $G_i$, where $\Omega_1 := \Omega^1_1 \setminus \{1\}$.
    
    Then $\Omega^1$ embeds into a group $G := \langle G(1) \mid \mathcal{R}\rangle $, given by a graded aspherical presentation and generated by $\Omega$, with the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\Omega_1^1$ embeds in a normal simple infinite subgroup $L$ of $G$ such that $G / L \cong H$;
        \item if $X \in L$ is not conjugate to any element of one of the groups $G_i$, 
        then either $X$ is equal to a power of an element of infinite order whose image in $H$ has even order, 
        or $X$ is of order dividing $m$ (of infinite order if $m = \infty$);
        \item the action by conjugation of $G$ on $L$ identifies $\operatorname{Aut} L \cong G$ (so $\operatorname{Out} L = H$).
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end obra-1 -->
<!-- obrb-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:B}
    Let $H$ and $G_i$ ($i \in I$, $|I| > 1$) be groups without involutions, the $G_i$ non-trivial; 
    let $\Omega^1$ be the free amalgam of $H$ and the $G_i$, $f$ any generating map on $\Omega$, and $m$ as in Theorem A. 
    Let $G$ and $L$ be the groups given by Theorem A for the factors $G_i$ and $H$, with $g_H = \operatorname{id}$ and the $g_i$ trivial.

    Then $\Omega^1$ embeds into $G$ and $\operatorname{Out} L \cong H$, and every $h\in H \setminus \{1 \}$ induces a regular automorphism on $L$.
<!-- end obrb-1 -->
<!-- obrd-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:D}
    Let $\{G_i\}_{i\in I}$, with $|I| > 1$, be a countable family of non-trivial countable groups without involutions (countable meaning finite or countably infinite). 
    Let $H$ be a countable group without involutions, and $m$ as in Theorem A.
    
    Then there is a generating map $f_\Omega$ for which the groups $G$ and $L$ of Theorem B are such that
    every proper subgroup of $L$ is either cyclic (of infinite order if $m=\infty$ and of order dividing $m$ otherwise) or contained in $\psi(G_i)$ for some $\psi \in \operatorname{Aut} L$ and $i \in I$.
<!-- end obrd-1 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma:conjugate-into}
    Let $G$ be the group of Theorem A with $m = \infty$. 
    Then every element of $G$ of finite order is conjugate to an element of one of the factors $G_i$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
